blocks.cap: Tanizaki Seiichi, who pours before he speaks

blocks.p: Tanizaki poured before he spoke. That was how Rei knew the matter was serious. The old man had spent forty years in Kita learning that nothing true gets said over an empty cup, and he had never once wasted the gesture on small business. The room above the shuttered tea shop smelled of roasted barley and of the river two streets over, the brown August smell of low tide and lantern wax that the whole district wore during Obon. Light came through the rice paper the colour of weak tea, flat and waiting.
He set Rei's cup down with both hands and folded his own around his.
"A man went into the Sumida three nights ago," he said. "He has not come up."
Rei waited. Tanizaki did not like to be hurried, and he did not like to be helped.
"It is not a police matter. It will not become one." The old man looked at the steam, not at Rei. "I need him found before the river gives him up on its own terms."

The drowned man's name was Kase. He was a fixer on the Grid side, a careful unregistered go-between who arranged for a thing to change hands without either hand being seen. Tanizaki had used him for thirty years, the way a man uses a tool he trusts so much he stops noticing it. Three nights ago Kase had sent word that he was holding something that frightened him. He wanted it off his hands and into Tanizaki's before Obon's gate opened all the way. Then he sent nothing. A Grid courier found his flat aired and empty, the kettle still warm, his shoes paired by the door.

"A man does not walk to the river barefoot in this season by accident," Tanizaki said. He turned his cup a quarter-turn on the table and did not drink. "And the Sumida in Obon does not keep what it takes in the ordinary way. It launches the dead all week. I would rather find Kase before the river decides he is one of them."

Both of Rei's registers stirred at that, low, the way they moved when something true was being undersold. Tanizaki was not asking him to recover a body. He was asking him to read one. He knew what reading a drowned man this week would pull through Rei, and he was asking anyway, and that alone was a measure of his fear. Tanizaki was the one person in Kita who never spent Rei carelessly. He had known Gin since Gin was a boy, and he had shaped Gin's whole field practice with exactly this restraint. Now he was pushing a cup across the table with a thing he wanted kept off the official books. Whatever Kase had been carrying, it reached further than one fixer's bad night by the water.
The rain had not started. Down toward the embankment, the first lantern sellers were setting out paper boats that no one had yet died recently enough to need.

After dark the river was a black road carrying small fires. Tōrō nagashi had begun upstream, and the lanterns came down in loose constellations. Each one was a paper box with a candle inside and a name brushed on the side, a family's grief made buoyant and sent out to float the dead home. Rei stood on the concrete embankment where the city's romance about the river ended and its plumbing began. He smelled diesel and silt and watched the little lights drift past him toward the bay.

This was the worst place to use his sight, and he had come here to use it. The membrane was at its thinnest all week, and nowhere thinner than over running water at the festival of the dead. The moment he let the first register open a hand's width, the whole surface of the Sumida tilted. It stopped being a river with lanterns on it. It became a procession, a long patient column of the departing moving with the current, and every paper flame was suddenly attended.

He walked downstream, listening for the wrong note in a song of the dead. A drowned man three nights gone was a wrong note. The properly dead were leaving this week. Kase was not leaving. Kase was held.

Rei felt him before he saw anything, the way fingers find a snag in cloth. It was down past the third pier, where the current went slack behind a concrete footing and the lanterns that drifted in turned slow circles and did not come out. His sight read the held place as cold. His skin read it as nothing at all. Something in that slack water was keeping a man the way the third basin had kept a half-made boy. It was not eating him, not yet. It was holding him, the way a person holds a thing they have not yet decided how to use.

And the held place was not silent. That was the part Tanizaki could not have prepared him for, the part both registers strained toward with their old forbidden appetite. It was leaking. A drowned man read this fresh still has his last quarter-hour in him, the way a struck bell holds its note. Rei could feel Kase's final minutes pressing out against the river's grip. The cold. The weight of his own coat. A decision. A hand that was or was not on the back of his neck. All of it waited down there to be looked at, and looking was exactly what thinned the wall, and the wall over this water was already thin enough to put his fingers through.
The lanterns turned their slow circles behind the pier. One of them, Rei noticed, had no name brushed on its side at all.

Kase was where Rei knew he would be. He hung in the slack behind the footing with one sleeve snagged on rebar, face down, turning slowly in the eddy, his coat as heavy as a drowned animal. Rei waded in to his knees and took his wrist.

The river did not fight him. That was the first wrong thing, and the worst. A body held three nights in slack water should belong to the river. Instead the current eased its grip the instant Rei committed to taking him, as if it had wanted him to have the body all along. Rei turned him over. Lantern light from upstream slid across a face that drowning had treated gently. It was slack and almost untroubled, the face of a careful man who had stopped being careful at the very end. Then the last quarter-hour, freed by Rei's touch, came off him into Rei's open register like cold off a stone.

Rei read it because he could not stop himself, and it was not what Tanizaki had sold him. Kase did not slip. Kase walked here barefoot in the dark with the thing that frightened him buttoned inside his coat. The thing was a list. It was a small ledger wrapped in waxed paper, a record of who in Kita had taken a particular kind of favour in the last two years, and what each favour had quietly cost the membrane to grant. Three nights too late, Kase had understood that carrying such a list made him a loose thread in something very large and very patient. The only place in the city thin enough to lose it, where no register could read it again, was the bottom of the Sumida in Obon. He did not drown himself out of fear. He drowned himself to hide the ledger where even the dead could not be made to give it up. He walked in unhurried, and this week the river was glad to keep them both.

And the keeper of the place was here. Rei had felt it the whole time, the way a watcher behind glass can be felt. It was not a demon and not a ghost. It was the slack water itself gone aware, a stretch of Obon river that had kept a hidden man and a hidden list for three nights and learned, the way standing water learns, the taste of keeping secrets. It did not want Kase. It wanted the warm thing now kneeling in its water with two registers open, a young man with a brother across the city that it could feel him aching toward. In its wordless way, it offered to hold for Rei too. It would take whatever he most needed hidden and keep it on the bottom, where no Healer and no Directorate and no patient brother-shaped thing could ever read it off him.
The ledger lay buttoned cold against the dead man's chest. The nameless lantern turned its slow circle by Rei's knee. The current waited to see what he would do with all three.

Rei gave the river nothing. He unbuttoned the coat with numb fingers, took the waxed packet out and pushed it inside his own shirt, against his skin, where it was his to carry. Whatever he needed hidden, he would carry that too. He said so out loud, to the water, and felt foolish, and said it again.

He got Kase out. That much he did not let himself negotiate. He laid him on the concrete above the tide line under a courier's tarp that Tanizaki's network kept cached for exactly such nights, and he knelt there dripping while the lanterns kept coming past the pier, name after name floating out toward a sea that could not read. The ledger sat heavy and cold against his chest. The slack water behind the footing had gone ordinary again. It was just river. The awareness in it had lapsed back into current the moment it failed to get what it offered to hold. Rei understood he would never be able to tell anyone whether he had outwitted it or had simply not been worth keeping.

Then there was the body, which was also the truth. A barefoot drowning in Obon was the most ordinary death in Tokyo. By morning a patrol would find him, and the municipal book would make him a sad seasonal number, and nobody would ever ask about a waxed ledger or the favours that cost the wall. Rei looked at the tarp and thought of the paired shoes by Kase's door. A man who left his shoes like that had already chosen how he wanted to go. He had wanted a lantern and a name. He had wanted to be off every book. Tanizaki had asked for the same thing over a cup he did not drink.

The rain finally started, fine and warm, dimpling the black water and guttering the nearer candles. Rei climbed the steps to the last lantern seller still packing her stall and bought the one plain lantern she had left. He borrowed her brush and wrote KASE on its side, badly, in a hand that would not stay steady. He lit it and set it on the water at the footing, beside the nameless one. He gave the river back the man and kept the secret. The two lanterns turned once together in the slack, and then the current took them both out into the procession. Kase left on his own terms.

Both registers were still half open and slow to close, the way they always were after running water. Through them Rei felt the shape of what he had really been doing down here. It was not a favour for an old man. He had come to the Sumida to practise the unbearable thing. To read a held person whom a patient power did not want to release. To take or refuse a hidden truth. To sit knee-deep in a thinned place and not be kept. Somewhere across the city his brother was held exactly like this, in slack water of a different kind, by a Healer glad to keep him. Rei did not yet have the nerve or the method to go in after him. Kase had been a rehearsal. The knowledge sat in him as cold as the river. He could perhaps find Gin the way he had found this man. Finding was the easy half. The water did not always give up what a person committed to taking.

blocks.cap: Tanizaki and Rei at dawn in the room above the tea shop

blocks.p: At dawn Tanizaki had set out two cups and filled three. It was the old form, the third for the one who had gone. He did not explain it and Rei did not ask. Rei came in soaked to the river line with the night still on him and told him what he had found, all of it. Then he took the waxed packet out of his shirt and laid it on the table between the cups.

Tanizaki listened the way he listened to everything, without moving, turning his cup the slow quarter-turn that meant he was rearranging forty years of a district to fit a new and terrible fact. He did not open the packet. He laid his palm flat on it for a while, like a man feeling for a pulse.

When he finally spoke, he said the thing Rei did not expect. Kase had carried for Gin too, years back, the same kind of quiet waxed errands. It was Gin who had taught the fixer the trick of hiding a thing in running water where no register could reach it. "If Kase chose the Sumida," Tanizaki said, "he chose it because your brother once told him it was the one safe place." Even a fixer's chosen drowning had Gin's careful handwriting in the margin.

He poured the third cup out on the floor, the smallest libation, and told Rei what the old give the young when they have nothing else. The river takes everyone on its own terms in the end. The only mercy available is to make the terms a person's own choosing. Kase had done that, which was more than most of the dead this week had managed.
Rei asked the question he had carried up the stairs. "Is there anyone who could go in after Gin? Someone stronger than me. Stronger than the CVD."
Tanizaki was quiet long enough for the barley smell to come back into the room. "You mean a Master," he said.

Rei had heard the word used loosely all his life, as praise for a good teacher. Tanizaki did not use it loosely. A Master, he said, was a Vanguard-rank independent. Someone who had climbed past what any institution could train and then stepped out of its reach. The CVD called them unreliable, and from the CVD's side of the desk they were. They chose their own cases. They needed long clearance time to stay stable at that height. They looked at patterns across years instead of weeks. And every one of them had paid something personal and specific to get there. "The capability and the cost are the same thing," Tanizaki said. "Your brother wrote that down. He had watched three of them up close."
"Then I go to one of them."

"You consult one of them," Tanizaki said. "You do not deploy them. That is the first rule, and people break it every year and come home with nothing. The exchange is real. Whatever you take from a Master, you give back something of the same weight, and they will know if you cheat. Their cost is visible if you look, so look, and do not pretend afterwards that you did not see it. And respect what they will not tell you. There is always something. It is always for a reason you would not like." He touched the packet again. "Gin said the three he knew were not manageable. Then he added that he was including himself in that."

He did not thank Rei in words. He slid four things across the table instead. The key to the safe house. The ward methodology, written in his own hand. The field profile he had kept on Gin since Gin was a boy, or the beginning of it, in a cardboard folder gone soft with handling. And a single sheet folded in three, in Gin's handwriting, with a title Rei could read through the paper.

"Outside the doctrine," Tanizaki said. "Your brother's list of the people who still do the old work. Priests, a shaman, an elder. Houses the CVD walks past every day. Do not read it today. You will know the day you need it."

These were the things he gave only at full trust. Rei understood that the drowned client had been, among everything else, the assessment. He had passed it the hard way, by being trusted with a death that had to stay off the book. The rain had stopped. The barley smell was back. Outside, the dead were mostly gone home and the lanterns had all reached the sea.

What stayed with Rei, walking out into the washed grey morning, was not the ledger or the key or even Kase's almost peaceful face. It was the small unbearable lesson the river had handed up with the body. Hiding is a kind of drowning. A held thing can be loved into staying held. His brother had taught a fixer the safe place, was now hidden in slack water of his own, and had known this trick from the inside long before the Healer ever wore his coat. Tonight Rei had rehearsed the exact shape of what he would have to do for Gin. He had learned its cost. He had learned that the water does not always give up what a person commits to taking. And he had decided to go in after him anyway.
The cup Tanizaki had poured for him had gone cold. He drank it. It would have been an insult, this morning, to leave anything the river could keep.

On the stairs down to the street he felt the folded sheet in his pocket, Gin's handwriting pressed against his hip through the cloth. He did not take it out. Tanizaki had said he would know the day. Rei had the uneasy feeling, going out into the grey, that the day was already on its way and walking faster than he was.
